extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Latin/classical literature (readers/students of Horace)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing Roman satirical poetry in the Horatian tradition: tone, diction, form, revision, audience, and legal/social limits. Focused on qualities Horace and his commentators treat as requisites of good satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Use humour suitably in satire; humour is a chief requisite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace speaks of the appropriate use of humour; 'Jesting oft cuts hard knots more forcefully and effectively than gravity.' Humour should be used to defend or expose, but with restraint and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity / terseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ brevity so that the thought runs on and is not encumbered by verbiage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You need terseness, that the thought may run on, and not become entangled in verbiage that weighs upon wearied ears; 'est brevitate opus, ut currat sententia.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness / clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain clearness of expression so the satire's point is intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Among requisites are clearness and purity of diction; avoid obscure or needlessly convoluted phrasing that confuses listeners/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of diction / plain style (genus tenue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer pure, plain diction characteristic of the genus tenue in poetry and oratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace praises 'purity of diction' and the 'plain style' (genus tenue) as distinctive of good satire, opposing the flashy or affected manner of low scribblers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness / polished composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for smooth, finished verse rather than rough, muddy flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace criticizes Lucilius for a 'muddy stream' and lack of finish; a good satirist should produce smooth composition and remove what 'trails beyond the proper limit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced mixture of grave and gay
rubrics_metrics.description: Blend seriousness and gaiety appropriately for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper mixture of the grave and the gay is required — a style now grave, often gay, in keeping with the role (orator, poet, wit) being assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tone to persona and restrain force
rubrics_metrics.description: Match tone to the speaker's role (orator, poet, wit) and restrain verbal force where wise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be 'now of orator or poet, at times of the wit, who holds his strength in check and husbands it with wisdom.' Do not expend all force at once; restrain for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target discerning critics, not the crowd
rubrics_metrics.description: Write to please a small circle of good critics rather than aiming for mass applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A writer should aim at pleasing, not the multitude, but a small circle of good critics; 'If he wins their approval, he may bid the cheap teachers of the lecture-room go hang!'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate mixing of Greek and Latin
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not gratuitously mingle Greek words with Latin; such mixture is a blemish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Magnum fecit, quod verbis Graeca Latinis miscuit' is derided — Horace calls such mixing a serious blemish in poetry and oratory and prefers harmonious, native diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast and over-ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from grandiloquent, bombastic style unsuitable for satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of poets like Bibaculus shows Horace's preference against pompous, lofty style ('turgidus...defingit Memnon') — satire should not adopt epic bombast but modest, fitting manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise and prune thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruthlessly revise: erase, prune, and polish until lines are worthy of rereading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Saepe stilum vertas' — often must you turn your pencil to erase, rewriting what is worthy of a second reading; prune what 'trails beyond the proper limit' and practice the 'art to blot.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid writing as rhetorical school exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write for the sake of rhetorical schools or cheap public recitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace rejects poems 'dictari in ludis' (dictated in common schools) — avoid producing verses aimed at schoolroom applause or formulaic exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe legal and social limits (avoid seditious/defamatory verses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of legal prohibitions and the danger of seditious or libelous writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trebatius warns 'You are forbidden to write bad — that is, seditious — verses against anyone.' Legal and political context can restrict satiric freedom; effective satire must avoid unlawful charges or invite suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possess nerve / spiritedness (have 'nerve' in verse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure verses have vigour and nerve rather than being 'nerveless.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics allege some of Horace's work is 'nerveless'; good satire should retain energy and conviction, not blandness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate appropriate models (Old Attic Comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study and, where fitting, imitate the robust blending of tones and techniques found in Old Attic Comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace recommends imitation of writers of Old Attic Comedy for their proper mixture of grave and gay and effective use of jesting; but avoid slavish copying of faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate 'molle atque facetum' — tenderness and charm
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for the qualities summarized as 'molle atque facetum' — a mild, graceful, witty plainness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace praises 'molle atque facetum' as distinctive of the plain style (genus tenue) — tenderness, grace, and wit that suit satirical purpose without coarseness.
